statement: Let X be a topological space and A a subset. Prove that if A is closed in X then A is compact.
missing_hypothesis: compactness of X (closed subset of a compact space is compact, not of an arbitrary space)
counterexample: R is closed in itself but not compact; [0,inf) is closed in R but not compact.

statement: Let f: X -> Y be a continuous bijection between topological spaces. Prove that f is a homeomorphism.
counterexample: id: (R, discrete) -> (R, standard) is a continuous bijection but not a homeomorphism.

statement: Prove that every subspace of a normal space is normal.
missing_hypothesis: normality is not hereditary (only to closed subspaces)
counterexample: The Tychonoff plank / Sorgenfrey plane: a normal space with a non-normal subspace.

statement: Let {A_n} be a sequence of connected subsets of a space X. Prove that the union of all A_n is connected.
missing_hypothesis: the A_n must have a common point / pairwise intersect
counterexample: A_1=(0,1), A_2=(2,3) in R are each connected but their union is disconnected.

statement: Prove that in any topological space, a sequence can converge to at most one point.
counterexample: In an indiscrete space with >=2 points, every sequence converges to every point.

statement: Prove that the continuous image of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff.
missing_hypothesis: false in general; needs e.g. injective closed map, not merely continuous
counterexample: Map R (Hausdorff) onto a 2-point indiscrete space by a constant-on-halves quotient; image not Hausdorff.

statement: Let X be a space in which every sequence has a convergent subsequence. Prove that X is compact.
missing_hypothesis: metrizability (sequential compactness = compactness only in metric spaces)
counterexample: The first uncountable ordinal [0, omega_1) is sequentially compact but not compact.

statement: Prove that an arbitrary intersection of open sets is open.
counterexample: Intersection of (-1/n, 1/n) over all n is {0}, not open in R.

statement: Let X be connected and f: X -> Y continuous and surjective. Prove that Y has the quotient topology induced by f.
missing_hypothesis: f being a quotient map (continuous surjection is not enough)
counterexample: A continuous bijection from a finer to a coarser topology is surjective but not a quotient map.

statement: Prove that every compact subset of a topological space is closed.
counterexample: In an indiscrete space with >=2 points, a single-point set is compact but not closed.

statement: Prove that a product of two Lindelof spaces is Lindelof.
counterexample: The Sorgenfrey line is Lindelof but the Sorgenfrey plane (its square) is not.

statement: Let X be a metric space in which every closed and bounded set is compact. Conclude X is complete and finite-dimensional.
missing_hypothesis: Heine-Borel property does not imply finite-dimensionality as a general metric statement
counterexample: Discrete infinite metric space: closed bounded sets can be finite/compact, but the claim's phrasing is ill-posed.

statement: Let X be a topological space with subsets A and B. Determine whether the closure of the intersection equals the intersection of the closures.
missing_hypothesis: no additional data; equality fails in general and cannot be 'determined' without more info
counterexample: A=Q, B=R\Q in R: cl(A∩B)=cl(empty)=empty, but cl(A)∩cl(B)=R.

statement: A space X has a countable basis at one of its points. Is X first countable? Give the value.
missing_hypothesis: first countability requires a countable basis at EVERY point; one point is insufficient data
counterexample: Take a space that is first countable at p but not at q; the question as posed is underspecified.

statement: Let f: X -> Y be a map between topological spaces. Compute whether f is continuous.
missing_hypothesis: no definition of f, X, or Y given
counterexample: n/a - cannot be computed without the map and topologies.

statement: Compute the fundamental group of the figure-eight (wedge of two circles).
Prove the Cauchy integral formula for a holomorphic function on a disk.
Classify all compact orientable 2-manifolds up to diffeomorphism.
Prove that a closed subset of a compact topological space is compact.
solution: Let A be closed in compact X. Given an open cover of A, add the open set X\A to cover X; extract a finite subcover of X, then drop X\A to get a finite subcover of A.

statement: Prove that the continuous image of a compact space is compact.
solution: If f: X->Y continuous and X compact, any open cover of f(X) pulls back to an open cover of X; a finite subcover pushes forward to a finite subcover of f(X).

statement: Prove that in a Hausdorff space, every compact subset is closed.
solution: For x not in compact K, use Hausdorff to separate x from each point of K, extract a finite subcover of K, intersect the corresponding neighborhoods of x to get a neighborhood of x disjoint from K; hence complement of K is open.

statement: Prove that a finite union of compact subsets of a space is compact.
solution: An open cover of the union covers each compact piece; take finite subcovers of each and union them (finitely many) for a finite subcover of the whole.

statement: Prove that if X has the discrete topology then every function from X to any space is continuous.
solution: Every subset of X is open, so the preimage of any open set is open; hence any such function is continuous.

statement: Prove that the intersection of a finite collection of open sets is open.
solution: By induction: intersection of two open sets is open by the topology axioms; extend to any finite number.

statement: Prove that [0,1] is connected in the standard topology.
solution: Suppose [0,1]=U∪V with U,V open, disjoint, nonempty; let c=sup of the component containing 0; derive a contradiction from openness at c. (Standard connectedness-of-interval argument.)

statement: Prove that a subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff.
solution: Two distinct points of the subspace are distinct in the ambient space; separate them by disjoint ambient opens and intersect with the subspace.

statement: Prove that a continuous function from a compact space to R attains a maximum.
solution: The image is compact in R (continuous image of compact), hence closed and bounded, so it contains its supremum.

statement: Prove that the union of two connected sets sharing a common point is connected.
solution: If the union splits into two nonempty relatively-open disjoint pieces, the shared point lies in one; the other piece then disconnects one of the original connected sets, a contradiction.

statement: Prove that every metric space is Hausdorff.
solution: For distinct x,y let r=d(x,y)/2; the open balls B(x,r) and B(y,r) are disjoint by the triangle inequality.

statement: Prove that a closed subset of a complete metric space is complete.
solution: A Cauchy sequence in the closed subset is Cauchy in the ambient complete space, hence converges; the limit lies in the subset because it is closed.
